How does multi-factor authentication differ from other forms of authentication, such as single-factor authentication or two-factor authentication?

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) is a security system that requires more than one method of authentication to verify the identity of a user. Single-factor authentication (SFA) only requires one method, such as a password, to authenticate a user's identity. Two-factor authentication (2FA) requires two methods, usually a password and a one-time code sent to a user's mobile device.

MFA is more secure than SFA or 2FA because it adds an additional layer of authentication, such as a biometric scan, security token, or smart card. This makes it more difficult for attackers to gain access to a user's account, even if they have obtained the user's password.

MFA is also more flexible than other forms of authentication because it allows organizations to choose which methods of authentication are appropriate for their specific security needs. Some organizations may require biometric scans for high-security applications, while others may only require a password and a security token for low-security applications.

Overall, MFA provides an added layer of security and flexibility that SFA and 2FA do not.
